To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the majority of patients undergoing epilepsy surgery have good outcome; 2) the most important factors in predicting outcome are the extent of the resection and the etiology of the epilepsy; and 3) the most common complications are transient and related to the surgical approach.

1) the use of MEG for the identification and removal of epileptogenic tissue is feasible and safe and 2) MEG-based “clusterectomy” is associated with a high probability of postoperative seizure freedom.

the use of a new surgical technique, the “infralateral transsylvian approach,” for mesial temporal epilepsy is associated with a lower risk for complications than the standard approach, but it does not result in better seizure outcome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the treatment of epilepsy, with the goal of improving the quality of life of patients with this disease.
the development and implementation of new methods of brain stimulation for the treatment of epilepsy.
the development of a novel, minimally invasive surgical technique for the treatment of epilepsy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a lot to learn and to do in the field of epilepsy surgery.
epilepsy surgery is a safe, efficacious, and well-established treatment for epilepsy.
epilepsy surgery is not a single entity but a complex and multifaceted field that requires a comprehensive and multidimensional approach.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the surgical treatment for epilepsy has evolved over the past 2 decades from the simple temporal lobe resection to a more complex surgery, which is tailored for each patient.

we are working on the development of new tools to help us to better understand the mechanisms of epilepsy, to help us to localize and treat it more effectively, and to help us to prevent its occurrence in the first place.
the use of the new imaging and surgical methods described in this issue of Neurosurgery will continue to improve outcomes and reduce complications for patients with epilepsy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a significant risk of complications after mesial temporal resection through the inferior temporal gyrus, but this approach is associated with excellent seizure outcomes.

the majority of the patients in the study had an improvement of at least one level on the SF-36 scale after surgery, and the majority of patients had a significant improvement in their quality of life.
we need to be able to identify and target epileptogenic networks.
